title: More Modular Exponential (MODP) Diffie-Hellman Groups for IKE
summary: Defines new Modular Exponential Diffie-Hellman groups for the Internet Key Exchange protocol. It documents the already widely used 1536-bit group 5 and adds larger groups numbered from 14, with sizes up to 8192 bits, and explains how the primes were chosen. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: Two people can agree on a secret number while others listen. They both use a big shared recipe. This memo lists some bigger and safer recipes of that kind.

questions: what are the ike modp groups
how big should a diffie-hellman group be
subtitle: Six standard prime groups, from 1536 to 8192 bits, for the Diffie-Hellman step in IKE.

tldr.problem: The four Diffie-Hellman groups defined for IKE are only about as strong as a 70-80 bit symmetric key, which is too weak for the Advanced Encryption Standard (AES). The widely used 1536-bit group 5 was also never formally defined.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC standardizes group 5 and defines five larger Modular Exponential (MODP) groups of 2048, 3072, 4096, 6144 and 8192 bits, numbered 14 to 18. Each is given as a fixed prime with generator 2.
tldr.outcome: IKE peers get a menu of stronger groups to choose from, and the RFC leaves the choice of group for each AES key size open. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted.

today: RFC 3526 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, so it remains the definition of these groups.

sections.title: Why IKE Needs Bigger Groups
sections.content:
The Internet Key Exchange (RFC 2409) negotiates a Diffie-Hellman group for certain cryptographic operations. IKE defined 4 groups, and the RFC says these are approximately as strong as a symmetric key of 70-80 bits.

The Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) needs stronger groups. For 128-bit AES the RFC cites a need for about a 3200-bit group, and for 192 and 256-bit keys about 8000 and 15400 bits. Other sources estimate 2500 and 4200 bits for the same two key sizes.

Because the estimates disagree, the RFC does not say which group goes with which AES key size. It only supplies groups. It stops at 8192 bits because, with the hardware of the time, bigger groups were too slow for practical use.
sections.eli5: Old locks were getting too easy to pick, so this memo offers bigger locks. Nobody agrees exactly how big is big enough, so it offers several sizes and lets you choose.

sections.title: The Six Groups
sections.content:
Section 2 documents the 1536-bit MODP group. Implementations had used it for a long time under the name group 5, even though RFC 2409 never defined it. The RFC standardizes that practice.

Sections 3 to 7 define new groups: 2048-bit as id 14, 3072-bit as id 15, 4096-bit as id 16, 6144-bit as id 17 and 8192-bit as id 18. For every group the generator is 2.

The RFC gives each prime both as a formula and as a hexadecimal value. The formula has the shape 2^n - 2^(n-64) - 1 + 2^64 * { [2^(n-130) pi] + k }, where k is a small number that differs per group (for example 741804 for the 1536-bit group).
sections.eli5: There are six recipes, numbered 5 and 14 through 18. Each one is a very long number written out in full, so two computers can be sure they use exactly the same one.

sections.title: How the Primes Are Chosen and Used
sections.content:
The primes follow the criteria established by Richard Schroeppel. All of them begin with the same leading digits in hexadecimal (FFFFFFFF FFFFFFFF C90FDAA2 2168C234 ...) and end with FFFFFFFF FFFFFFFF, because each is built from the digits of pi plus a small offset.

The RFC also gives guidance on the secret exponent used in the calculation. It must be chosen so that it is not the weakest link in the system, and it should have double the entropy of the strength of the whole system. For a group of 128-bit strength, that means more than 256 bits of randomness in the exponent.
sections.eli5: The big numbers are built from a famous never-ending number, pi, so nobody can claim they hid a trick in them. The secret you pick should be at least twice as random as the lock is strong.

sections.title: Strength Estimates
sections.content:
The RFC stresses that group strengths are always estimates, and there are as many methods to estimate them as there are cryptographers. It therefore gives two estimates per group, taken from both ends of the scale, so the true strength is likely between them.

Each estimate comes with a minimum exponent size. For group 14 (2048-bit), the strength is 110 to 160 bits, with exponents of at least 220 and 320 bits. For group 18 (8192-bit), the range is 190 to 310 bits.
sections.eli5: Nobody can say exactly how hard each lock is to break, so the memo gives a low guess and a high guess for each. The real answer is somewhere in between.

sections.title: IANA Registry Changes
sections.content:
IKE defined 4 Diffie-Hellman groups, numbered 1 through 4. This document defines a new group 5 and new groups 14 to 18.

Further groups are requested through "IETF Consensus" as defined in RFC 2434. In practice, the RFC says new groups are expected to be documented in a Standards Track RFC.
sections.eli5: The official list of recipe numbers now has new entries. To add another one, you have to write it up properly and get the community to agree.
